Qualification Frameworks Compared

The Commercial SystemPart 20

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Revenue

In short: A sales qualification framework is a fixed set of questions a seller must answer, with evidence from the buyer, before a deal is treated as real. The common ones test different things. BANT checks whether the buyer can buy now. CHAMP starts from the buyer's problem. MEDDICC maps how the buying organisation will decide. SPICED tests whether the problem is urgent enough to act on. Benchmark data suggests that teams which apply any framework consistently outperform those which do not, and that the framework matters less than whether its answers decide stage movement. Pick the one that matches the deal you sell, then make every letter a field.

Key points

  • Forrester's 2024 buying survey found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase and 86% of B2B purchases stalling, which is the problem complex-deal frameworks were built for.
  • In a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities, top performers were 588% more likely to follow a qualification methodology effectively, a relative figure without a published baseline.
  • The same data found SPICED reached high completion in fewer meetings than MEDDPICC, while deals completing either one by the solution stage were roughly three times more likely to win.
  • Up to 60% of lost deals end in no decision, according to research on 2.5 million sales conversations, and no common framework tests for buyer indecision directly.
  • A framework only changes outcomes when each element is a CRM field with evidence and a condition for moving stage.

Most sales teams have a qualification framework in name. Fewer have one in practice. The letters appear in onboarding slides and in the pipeline review, but the CRM holds a stage, an amount and a close date, and the qualification is in the seller's head.

The choice of framework is usually made by whoever joined from a firm that used one. This piece compares the main frameworks by what they actually test, sets out what the evidence says about using them, and gives a way to choose. The explainers on MEDDICC and BANT cover each framework's elements in detail; this piece does not repeat them.

The problem qualification has to solve

Qualification exists because selling time is scarce and most opportunities do not close. Two features of current B2B buying make it harder than it was.

The first is the size of the buying group. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024, a survey of more than 16,000 business buyers, found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, with 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments and 86% stalling at some point. Forrester also reported that 81% of buyers were dissatisfied with the provider they chose. A framework that asks only whether "the decision maker" is engaged is asking about one person in thirteen.

The second is that buyers do much of their evaluation without a seller present. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Qualification signals that once came from conversation now have to be inferred from fewer, later meetings.

Forrester has argued for some time that the unit of qualification should be the buying group, not the lead. Its analysts report that fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, and that clients who delivered three or more buying group members to sales saw a 50% increase in meeting-to-closed-won conversion.

What each framework tests

The frameworks are not competing answers to one question. Each was built for a different kind of deal, and each tests a different risk.

FrameworkElementsWhat it testsFits bestMain gap
BANTBudget, Authority, Need, TimelineWhether this buyer can buy nowTransactional and mid-market deals with one or two decision makersAssumes a known budget and a single authority; weak on buying groups
CHAMPChallenges, Authority, Money, PrioritisationWhether the problem is real and ranked, before money is discussedSolution sales where budget is created after the problem is agreedLight on how the buyer will decide
MEDDICC and MEDDPICCMetrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, (Paper process), Identify or implicate pain, Champion, CompetitionHow the buying organisation will decide and signComplex enterprise deals with several functions and procurementSlower to complete; can become a form-filling exercise
SPICEDSituation, Pain, Impact, Critical event, DecisionWhether the problem is urgent enough to act on nowRecurring-revenue sales where the case for change is the hard partLess explicit about procurement and competition

MEDDIC was developed at PTC in 1996, according to the training firm that now teaches it, and later gained Competition and Paper Process to become MEDDPICC. Its own definition of Paper Process, the steps from decision to signature, describes it as where many deals are lost, usually in legal and procurement. That is the clearest sign of the framework's purpose: it was built to make a forecast survive contact with a buyer's contracting process.

SPICED, associated with the consultancy Winning by Design, puts the critical event, the date by which the buyer must act, at the centre. BANT's Timeline element asks a similar question, but SPICED asks why the date exists, which is the better test of whether it will hold.

What the evidence says about using them

Independent evidence comparing frameworks head to head is thin. The most detailed public data comes from Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmark, a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities and more than a million hours of recorded conversations across 530 companies. Its figures are relative multipliers without published baselines, so treat them as direction rather than measurement.

Finding (Ebsta and Pavilion, 2023 data)Figure reported
Top performers following a qualification methodology effectively588% more likely than others
Top performers with the economic buyer engaged before the solution was presented489% more likely
Meetings and contacts to reach above 80% completion, SPICED4.7 meetings, 3.4 contacts
Meetings and contacts to reach above 80% completion, MEDDPICC5.6 meetings, 5.2 contacts
Win likelihood for deals completing the framework by the solution stageSPICED 307% more likely, MEDDPICC 324% more likely
Effect of spending 50% longer than average in qualification120% more likely to slip

Two readings follow. First, the gap between the two frameworks' win effects is small next to the gap between completing one and not completing either. Consistency matters more than the choice. Second, MEDDPICC asks for more contacts because it maps more of the buying group. That is its cost and its point: if the deal really involves 13 people, a framework that completes after three contacts has probably missed some.

The evidence also shows what no framework covers well. Dixon and McKenna's research on about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found that 40–60% of lost deals were lost to indecision, with about half of all losses ending in no decision. Calls with high buyer indecision were won about 6% of the time. A buyer can pass every letter of MEDDICC and still fail to decide. Pain, critical events and champions are proxies for decisiveness; none measures it.

The framework matters less than the rule that a deal cannot move stage until its answers are written down.

How to choose

The choice should follow the shape of the deals, not the background of the sales leader. Three questions settle most cases.

How many people sign? If one or two people decide and buy within a quarter, BANT or CHAMP is enough, and MEDDPICC will slow sellers down for little gain. If several functions and procurement are involved, a framework that maps the decision process and paper process earns its extra meetings.

Where are deals lost? Look at the last two quarters of closed-lost reasons (see What is a closed-lost reason?). If deals die in procurement, Paper Process matters. If they die in no decision, the critical event and the size of the impact matter more. If they die on price, the economic buyer and metrics were probably never established.

What can the team sustain? A seven-element framework that sellers complete half-way is worse than a four-element one they complete fully. Ebsta's completion figures suggest that the bigger framework needs about one more meeting and two more contacts per deal.

Some firms run two: a light framework for smaller deals and a full one above a deal-size threshold. That works if the threshold is written down and the CRM enforces which fields apply.

Make every letter a field

A framework changes outcomes only when it governs stage movement. The practical build has four parts, and each one is a small change to the CRM rather than a training programme.

Each element becomes a field with a short evidence note, not a tick box. "Economic buyer: identified" says little; "Economic buyer: CFO, met 12 March, confirmed budget owner" can be checked.

Stage exit criteria name the elements that must be complete before a deal moves. The explainer on pipeline stage definitions covers how to write them. A deal in the proposal stage with no decision criteria recorded is a forecast risk, and the CRM should show it.

Disqualification is recorded as a decision. When a seller drops an opportunity, the reason, owner and date go on the record. That turns qualification from a filter into data: after a quarter, the firm can see which elements most often fail and in which segments. This is the decision-record discipline from The commercial decisions worth recording applied to the earliest decision in the funnel.

Completion is reviewed against outcomes. Once a quarter, compare framework completion on won deals with completion on lost ones. If they look the same, the framework is being filled in after the fact.

Illustrative example: changing frameworks by deal size
Decision
Replace a single BANT checklist with BANT below a set deal size and MEDDPICC above it.
Reason and owner
Closed-lost review showed most large deals dying in procurement and no decision, neither of which BANT tests. Agreed by the revenue leader; owned by revenue operations.
What changed
Paper process and critical event became required fields for large deals before the proposal stage. The firm agreed to review win rates by band after two quarters before deciding whether to keep the split.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size software firm selling to mid-market and enterprise buyers, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Choose by deal shape. BANT and CHAMP suit small buying groups; MEDDPICC suits deals that pass through procurement; SPICED suits deals where urgency is the hard part.
  • Consistency beats selection. The benchmark gap between using a framework and not using one is far larger than the gap between frameworks.
  • No framework tests indecision. Track no-decision losses separately and treat critical events and impact as the nearest proxies.
  • Fields, not slides. Each element needs an evidence note and a role in stage exit criteria.
Gateway card

Before you adopt or change a qualification framework

  • Last two quarters of closed-lost reasons grouped by where deals died
  • Typical number of people involved in your buyers' decisions, by segment
  • One framework chosen per deal band, with the band threshold written down
  • Each element added as a CRM field with an evidence note
  • Stage exit criteria updated to name required elements
  • A quarterly review comparing framework completion on won and lost deals

Common questions

What is the difference between BANT and MEDDICC?

BANT checks whether a buyer has the budget, authority, need and timeline to buy now. MEDDICC maps how the buying organisation will decide, including its metrics, economic buyer, criteria, process, pain, champion and competitors, and suits complex deals with several decision makers.

Which sales qualification framework is best?

None is best for every deal. Lighter frameworks such as BANT suit small buying groups and short cycles, while MEDDPICC suits enterprise deals that pass through procurement. Applying one consistently matters more than which one you choose.

What does SPICED stand for in sales?

SPICED stands for Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical event and Decision. It focuses on whether the buyer's problem is urgent enough to act on by a specific date.

How do you make a sales team actually use a qualification framework?

Turn each element into a CRM field with an evidence note, make named elements a condition for moving a deal to the next stage, and review framework completion on won and lost deals each quarter.

Sources and notes

  • Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs, December 2024. Analyst press release; source of the 13-person, 89%, 86% and 81% figures.
  • Forrester, The State Of Business Buying 2024, December 2024. Analyst blog; survey of more than 16,000 business buyers.
  • Forrester, Saying Goodbye to MQLs, November 2023, by Simon Daniels. Analyst blog; client conversion figures are not independently audited.
  • Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience, March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025.
  • Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks, 2024. Vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities; relative figures without published baselines.
  • MEDDICC, Who Created MEDDIC?. Published by a training firm that sells the method; origin claims not independently verified.
  • MEDDICC, MEDDPICC. Training firm's definitions of each element.
  • Challenger, How to Overcome Customer Indecision Using the JOLT Effect Approach, February 2024. Summary of Dixon and McKenna's research on about 2.5 million sales conversations; published by a training firm.

Next Move

Take the last ten deals your team lost and mark, for each, which framework element was missing or wrong at the time. The element that appears most often is the one your current framework, or your use of it, is not testing.
